stories.headline: British Local and Regional Elections Test Starmer's Leadership and Farage's Rise
stories.summary:
Voters across England, Scotland, and Wales cast ballots Thursday in local council and regional elections widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Keir Starmer's Labour government, less than a year after Labour swept to power in the 2024 general election. The results are expected to reflect deep public frustration with Starmer over issues including cost-of-living pressures, welfare cuts, and a perceived lack of policy momentum.

The elections are also a major test for Nigel Farage's Reform UK party, which has surged in national polls and is seeking to translate that support into tangible electoral gains at the local level. Strong Reform showings could signal a fundamental realignment in British politics, putting pressure on both Labour and the Conservatives simultaneously.

For Starmer, significant losses could trigger internal party pressure and calls to change direction ahead of the next general election. Analysts describe the vote as one of the most consequential rounds of local elections in recent British history, with results expected to come in through Friday morning.

stories.headline: Five Killed in Fire at Packed Mexico Fairground Concert Attended by Tens of Thousands
stories.summary:
At least five people died and scores were injured Thursday after a massive fire broke out at a crowded fairground in Villahermosa, in Mexico's Tabasco state. The blaze erupted during a concert in the early morning hours, with local officials reporting that as many as 135,000 people were in attendance when the fire started.

Social media footage showed panicked crowds fleeing the fairgrounds as flames spread. The cause of the fire has not been determined. Emergency services eventually brought the blaze under control, according to Tabasco Governor Javier May, who posted an update on X and expressed condolences to victims' families.

Governor May announced an economic recovery program for businesses affected by the fire and said state authorities would provide full support to victims. The incident is one of the deadliest crowd-event disasters in Mexico in recent years, raising questions about safety protocols at large public gatherings.

stories.headline: FEMA Review Council Recommends Sweeping Overhaul, Including Privatizing Flood Insurance and Shifting Power to States
stories.summary:
The FEMA Review Council, established by President Trump to examine the agency's structure and effectiveness, approved its final report Thursday, recommending a broad restructuring of the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Key proposals include reviewing and reducing agency staffing levels, devolving greater disaster-response responsibility to state, local, and tribal governments, and privatizing the National Flood Insurance Program.

The recommendations represent a significant philosophical shift in how the federal government approaches disaster recovery — moving away from a centralized federal response model toward one that relies more heavily on state and local capacity. Critics of the current system have long argued that FEMA is bloated and slow; defenders counter that smaller and poorer states lack the resources to handle major disasters without robust federal support.

The report's implementation would require action by Congress and the executive branch. Advocates of the changes argue they would increase efficiency and reduce federal spending, while opponents warn that shifting responsibility to states could leave vulnerable communities without adequate assistance in the aftermath of large-scale disasters.

stories.headline: OpenAI Releases Expanded Access to Cybersecurity-Focused GPT-5.5 Model for Vetted Defenders
stories.summary:
OpenAI announced Thursday it is opening a limited preview of a more permissively licensed version of its GPT-5.5 model, internally known as "Spud," to vetted cybersecurity professionals and defenders. The release comes amid security testing that suggests GPT-5.5 is nearly as capable as Anthropic's Mythos Preview model at identifying and exploiting software vulnerabilities.

The rapid advancement of AI models capable of finding and weaponizing software bugs has intensified debate in Silicon Valley and at the White House over how to prevent such tools from reaching malicious actors. OpenAI's decision to limit access to screened cyber defenders represents an attempt to balance the defensive utility of the technology against the risk of misuse.

Separately, a senior Pentagon technology official said Thursday the Defense Department would not return to an exclusive reliance on any single AI vendor, pointedly ruling out a renewed sole-source relationship with Anthropic. "Never again will we be single-threaded with any one model," said Emil Michael, under secretary of Defense for research and engineering, at the AI+ Expo.

stories.headline: Gaza Ceasefire on Brink of Collapse as Hamas Disarmament Talks Stall
stories.summary:
Ceasefire negotiations between Israel and Hamas have reached a deadlock, with Israeli media reporting that Israel is preparing to resume fighting in Gaza. An Israeli airstrike this week killed the son of Hamas's chief negotiator Khalil al-Hayya, and Palestinian sources confirmed to the BBC that talks have stalled over Hamas's refusal to disarm.

Israel contends that Hamas's stance on disarmament violates the ceasefire agreement that took effect October 10. Israeli Prime Minister adviser Michael Eisenberg told the BBC that 'all options are on the table,' while Israel's Channel 12 News reports Washington may give Israel a 'green light' to resume operations, potentially expanding the so-called Yellow Line that marks roughly 60 percent of Gaza under Israeli military control.

Hamas insists Israel is the party in violation, citing failures to meet humanitarian commitments and continued deadly strikes. At least 846 people have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire began, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Israel says five of its soldiers have been killed in the same period. More than two million residents remain displaced.

Civilians in Gaza expressed exhaustion and fear of renewed full-scale war. One displaced mother called on Hamas to consider disarmament, while a neighbor accused Israel of 'intransigence' and warned that with global attention focused on conflicts in Iran and Lebanon, Gaza risks sliding back into fighting with little international scrutiny.

stories.headline: FBI Reportedly Opens Criminal Investigation Into Reporter Who Wrote About Kash Patel's Drinking
stories.summary:
The FBI has reportedly launched a criminal investigation into whether classified or sensitive information was leaked to Sarah Fitzpatrick, a reporter for The Atlantic who wrote that FBI Director Kash Patel's 'excessive drinking' was causing deep concern within the bureau. The investigation was reportedly ordered from Patel's executive suite, with a unit in Huntsville, Alabama, directed to review Fitzpatrick's contacts, phone metadata, and social media activity.

The FBI's assistant director flatly denied the report, saying in a statement: 'This is completely false. No such investigation like this exists. The reporter you mention is not being investigated at all.' Patel previously sued The Atlantic for $250 million over the drinking story, denying he had ever been intoxicated on the job. The Atlantic on Thursday published an update to its original story that included a photo of custom bourbon bottles bearing Patel's name that he reportedly gives out.

Carol Leonnig, the senior investigative reporter who broke the investigation story, said her outlet stands by its reporting and cited multiple sources. She noted that FBI agents within the bureau have themselves raised concerns about whether any legal predicate exists to open such an investigation, as leak investigations typically require a reasonable belief that classified information was disclosed.

The episode raises significant press freedom concerns. Critics argue that using the FBI's investigative apparatus to pursue a reporter who wrote critically about the bureau's director would represent a serious threat to journalistic independence. Supporters of Patel contend that legitimate leak investigations are lawful and that the original story relied on anonymous sources making unverified claims.

stories.headline: Rubio Announces New Sanctions on Cuba's Military-Controlled Business Empire
stories.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Thursday a fresh round of sanctions targeting Cuba's military-industrial enterprise, including GAESA — Grupo de Administración Empresarial S.A. — an umbrella conglomerate controlled by the Cuban military that dominates the island's economy. The sanctions also target GAESA's leader and a state-owned natural resources company.

The measures were imposed under President Trump's May 1 executive order targeting those responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security. The action signals that the Trump administration is actively pursuing its long-stated goal of regime change in Cuba, a priority shared by Rubio, who has long championed a hard line against Havana.

GAESA controls large portions of Cuba's tourism, retail, and import sectors, meaning the sanctions are designed to cut off a primary revenue stream for the Cuban government and military. The Biden administration had moved to ease some Cuba restrictions, a course the Trump administration has sharply reversed.

stories.headline: Rwandan Government Critic and Singer Dies Moments Before Prison Release, Sparking Suspicion
stories.summary:
Rwandan singer and YouTuber Aimable Karasira, 48, died Wednesday as he was being escorted out of Nyarugenge Prison in Kigali, just moments before his scheduled release. The Rwanda Correctional Service said he died at a hospital after allegedly overdosing on prescription medication, and announced a post-mortem examination. Karasira suffered from diabetes, high blood pressure, and poor mental health, according to prison officials.

Karasira was well known for YouTube videos criticizing President Paul Kagame's government and the ruling Rwandan Patriotic Front. He was arrested in 2021 and sentenced in 2025 to five years for inciting division, though a high court had acquitted him of more serious charges including genocide denial. Human rights activists and government critics immediately called his death suspicious, noting that it occurred at the precise moment of his release.

Rwandan human rights activist Denise Zaneza, based in Belgium, called for an independent investigation, citing what she described as Rwanda's history of repression and suspicious deaths in detention. She drew a parallel to the 2020 prison death of gospel singer Kizito Mihigo, another RPF critic and genocide survivor whose death the government also ruled a suicide. Both cases have drawn international scrutiny over press freedom and political repression in Rwanda.

Karasira's criticism centered on RPF killings of Tutsi civilians during the 1994 genocide — a narrative that challenges the Rwandan government's official account of the period. The government has not responded to calls for an independent autopsy.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. and Iran Edge Toward Short-Term Deal to Halt War, White House Awaits Tehran Response
stories.summary:
The United States and Iran are moving closer to a temporary agreement to end their war, with Washington presenting Tehran a one-page memorandum of understanding that would halt fighting, limit Iran's nuclear program, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping. President Trump told reporters the two sides have had "very good talks over the last 24 hours" and expressed confidence a deal is possible within days, though he cautioned "we are not far, but there is no deal yet." U.S. officials said they expected an Iranian response within 24 to 48 hours.

The proposed MOU would set a framework for more detailed nuclear negotiations rather than resolve all outstanding issues immediately. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian confirmed he met with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has remained in hiding since the war began, as Tehran deliberates over the 14-point American proposal. China's foreign minister Wang Yi, meeting with his Iranian counterpart in Beijing, called for the Strait to be reopened "as soon as possible" and described a lasting ceasefire as an "urgent priority," adding pressure on Iran to respond.

Supporters of the deal, including some Republican hawks and Gulf allies, argue a negotiated end to the conflict would stabilize global energy markets and avert further escalation. Critics on both sides remain skeptical: some conservatives warn any deal must include ironclad nuclear verification mechanisms, while Iranian hardliners have resisted what they characterize as capitulation to American military pressure. A PBS/NPR/Marist poll released Thursday found six in ten Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled the Iran conflict.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio separately met Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican for two and a half hours to discuss "efforts to achieve a durable peace in the Middle East," following a public clash between President Trump and the American-born pontiff over the war. The 60-day clock on the 1973 War Powers Resolution has expired, with Congress pressing the administration for justification for continuing Operation Epic Fury. Oil prices have fallen and stocks surged on reports of deal progress, though analysts warn pump prices will likely remain elevated for months even if the Strait reopens immediately.

stories.headline: Update: Three Australian Women Linked to Islamic State Arrested on Return from Syrian Detention Camps
stories.summary:
Australian federal police arrested three women with alleged ties to the Islamic State on Thursday as they returned home after years of detention in Syrian camps, executing a plan that had been the subject of intense political debate. Kawsar Abbas, 53, and Zeinab Ahmed, 31, were taken into custody on arrival in Melbourne, while Janai Safar, 32, was arrested after landing in Sydney. A fourth woman in the group was not arrested. The party also included nine children, ranging in age from approximately six years old to mid-teens, who are to receive psychological support and be assessed for possible radicalisation.

The group had been held at al-Roj camp in Syria since 2019. Abbas is married to a man Australian police suspect of funneling funds to IS through a charity, a charge he denied. Safar, a former Sydney nursing student, traveled to Syria in 2015 and told a newspaper in 2019 she had gone of her own accord. The widow of a notorious IS recruiter, believed to be Zahra Ahmed, was the only woman among those who arrived who was not arrested; she was shielded from cameras by a group of about 15 men at Melbourne airport before being driven away.

Potential charges include terrorism offences including entering or remaining in a declared area. Police Commissioner Krissy Barratt had confirmed Wednesday that some of the women would be charged upon arrival. Australia had maintained it would provide no government assistance to help the women return, making the episode politically fraught for the Labor government.

Australia is among several Western nations grappling with what legal and humanitarian obligations they bear toward citizens — and especially the children of citizens — who traveled to join IS or were born in the caliphate. Human rights organizations have argued the children in particular face life-threatening conditions in Syrian detention and deserve repatriation regardless of their parents' alleged offenses. The arrests mark one of the most significant IS-related counterterrorism actions in Australia in recent years.

stories.headline: South Africa Denies 'Fake' Xenophobia Videos as Multiple African Nations Demand Answers
stories.summary:
South Africa's government on Thursday condemned the circulation of what it called fabricated videos purporting to show vigilante attacks on foreign nationals, as a diplomatic dispute over alleged xenophobia spread across the continent. Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni told reporters following a cabinet meeting that the footage was "intended to undermine the good reputation of South Africa internationally" but did not specify which videos she was addressing. Ghana has written to the African Union requesting a fact-finding mission and describing the situation as a "serious risk to the safety and wellbeing" of Africans in South Africa, invoking principles of "African solidarity and brotherhood."

Nigeria has raised the issue formally and offered to repatriate its nationals, while Kenya, Malawi, Lesotho, and Zimbabwe have all issued warnings to citizens residing in South Africa. The dispute was sparked by videos shared online roughly two weeks ago appearing to show vigilante groups challenging people they believed to be undocumented migrants; in one clip, a Ghanaian man was reportedly told to "fix his country" and leave. Thousands of South Africans have staged largely peaceful protests in major cities demanding the mass deportation of undocumented foreign nationals, citing concerns about jobs, housing, and crime.

South Africa's government acknowledged citizens' right to protest illegal immigration but reiterated that violence is unacceptable. President Cyril Ramaphosa's spokesperson said he had emphasized that "South Africa is a welcoming country" and rejected characterizations suggesting otherwise. South African authorities said there have been no official reports of looting of foreign-owned shops or physical attacks accompanying the current wave of demonstrations.

Xenophobic violence has a long and deadly history in South Africa, with major outbreaks in 2008 and 2019 resulting in deaths and mass displacement of migrants from neighboring countries. The current episode is drawing unusual multilateral diplomatic pressure, including a call for AU intervention that could have consequences for South Africa's regional relationships and its ambitions to lead pan-African initiatives.

stories.headline: China Sentences Two Former Defence Ministers to Death With Reprieve on Corruption Charges
stories.summary:
A Chinese military court on Thursday sentenced former defence ministers Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu to suspended death sentences — effectively life imprisonment without parole — on bribery charges, state media reported. Both men had their personal assets confiscated. The sentences follow years of investigation and are among the most prominent outcomes of President Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption campaign within the People's Liberation Army.

Wei served as defence minister from 2018 to 2023. Li succeeded him but was abruptly dismissed in October 2023 after disappearing from public life for two months, prompting widespread speculation. Investigators found both men had accepted large sums in bribes and used their positions to benefit associates.

The verdicts come after Xi publicly acknowledged the military crackdown in February, stating the army had undergone 'revolutionary tempering in the fight against corruption.' The purge has extended to the country's top military general, Zhang Youxia, who was also recently removed. Critics of Xi argue the anti-corruption drives serve a dual purpose, also functioning as a tool to eliminate political rivals and consolidate personal control over the military.

stories.headline: BJP Aide Assassinated Amid Post-Election Violence in West Bengal
stories.summary:
Chandranath Rath, personal assistant to senior BJP leader Suvendu Adhikari, was shot dead Wednesday night in West Bengal, India, becoming at least the third person killed in political violence since the state election results were announced Monday. Rath was traveling home when a gunman fired from a motorcycle. Police recovered live rounds and spent cartridges but made no arrests, though more than 400 people had already been detained in connection with earlier post-election incidents.

The killing comes days after the BJP secured a historic landslide in West Bengal, winning 207 of 294 seats and ending 15 years of rule by Mamata Banerjee's Trinamool Congress. Adhikari, widely expected to be sworn in as chief minister on Saturday, called the killing 'cold-blooded murder.' The TMC condemned the violence but both parties have accused each other of targeting their respective workers.

Tensions had been building before results were announced, stemming from a controversial voter roll cleansing exercise that Banerjee alleged removed non-BJP voters. Election officials denied the claims. The assassination of a senior aide to the likely incoming chief minister has sharply escalated fears of broader unrest as the state prepares for a transfer of power.

stories.headline: Tornadoes Tear Through Mississippi, Collapsing Hundreds of Homes and Injuring at Least 17
stories.summary:
At least 14 tornadoes were reported across central and western Mississippi on Wednesday night, with one confirmed by the National Weather Service. The storms collapsed hundreds of homes, downed trees, and knocked out power across multiple counties. At least 17 people were reported injured, and a 1-year-old child was reported missing in Lincoln County as of early Thursday.

The National Weather Service described one system as 'a very large and dangerous tornado' that tracked from Lincoln County into Lawrence County. In Bogue Chitto, falling trees split a car and trapped residents at a mobile home park. A separate home in Tylertown was engulfed by fire after a lightning strike. Governor Tate Reeves confirmed the scale of destruction and said the state Emergency Management Agency was coordinating response efforts.

More severe weather, including the possibility of additional tornadoes, was forecast Thursday across parts of Alabama, Georgia, Florida, the Carolinas, and Texas. Damage assessments were ongoing in Lincoln County, with authorities asking residents to stay off roads as emergency crews worked to clear blocked passages.

stories.headline: Update: Israel Strikes Beirut as U.S. Reports Iran Deal Near, Blockade Continues
stories.summary:
Israel launched airstrikes on Beirut's southern suburbs for the first time since a ceasefire was announced April 16, targeting what Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described as a Hezbollah commander. The strikes came amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, with Trump telling reporters that U.S.-Iran talks had been productive over the last 24 hours and that a deal was potentially close.

A U.S. media report indicated the Trump administration was near finalizing a memorandum of understanding with Iran, with a response from Tehran expected within 48 hours. Iran's foreign ministry said a U.S. proposal was still under consideration, and Iran's navy signaled the Strait of Hormuz could reopen if what it called "aggressors' threats" ended. The U.S. blockade remains fully in effect, with U.S. Central Command announcing 52 ships have been turned around so far.

The U.S. also reported disabling an Iranian-flagged oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman. The developments mark a significant intensification and diplomatic pivot within the same 24-hour window, with active military operations continuing even as negotiators reportedly close in on a framework agreement.

The situation remains highly fluid. Supporters of the administration's pressure campaign argue the blockade and military actions have brought Iran closer to a deal; critics warn that simultaneous Israeli strikes on Lebanon risk derailing diplomacy and broadening the conflict across the region.

stories.headline: North Korea Amends Constitution to Give Kim Jong Un Sole Legal Authority Over Nuclear Arsenal
stories.summary:
North Korea has revised its constitution to formally vest sole authority over the country's nuclear weapons in leader Kim Jong Un, according to South Korean lawmakers briefed by Seoul's National Intelligence Service. The change codifies what had long been Kim's de facto control, but its formal enshrinement in the country's foundational law signals a deliberate and permanent posture regarding the arsenal.

Pyongyang accompanied the announcement with a statement that its status as a nuclear-armed state "will not change based on external rhetorical claims," a clear signal directed at the United States and any ongoing diplomatic overtures. The constitutional amendment removes any ambiguity about succession or institutional checks on nuclear decision-making.

The move has significant implications for nonproliferation efforts and for any future negotiations. Analysts note that formalizing Kim's singular authority makes denuclearization commitments harder to negotiate and enforce, as no other official or body retains legal standing to offer concessions on the arsenal.

stories.headline: Hantavirus Outbreak Spreads Beyond Cruise Ship as WHO Confirms Cases in Multiple Countries
stories.summary:
A hantavirus outbreak that began aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius has now spread to patients in the Netherlands, Switzerland, and is under investigation in South Africa, the World Health Organization confirmed. Three passengers have died since the ship departed Argentina a month ago, and the WHO has identified eight cases — three confirmed, five suspected — among people connected to the vessel. The MV Hondius is now sailing toward Spain's Canary Islands after three days anchored near Cape Verde.

The South African Andes strain of hantavirus — which has previously been observed spreading between human patients, an unusual characteristic for the virus — was identified in two confirmed cases. A KLM flight attendant in Amsterdam was separately hospitalized with hantavirus symptoms after contact with a Dutch passenger who later died, raising concern about transmission beyond the ship's passenger and crew population.

U.S. health authorities in Georgia and Arizona confirmed they are monitoring three returned passengers, all currently asymptomatic. The multinational spread of cases across passengers from at least 23 countries has prompted the WHO to issue guidance and monitor the situation closely. Hantavirus carries a high fatality rate and no approved antiviral treatment, making containment of human-to-human transmission a priority for public health officials.

stories.headline: Update: Federal Judge Rules Justice Department May Keep Seized Fulton County 2020 Election Ballots
stories.summary:
A federal judge ruled Wednesday that the Justice Department does not have to return 2020 presidential election ballots and other materials seized by the FBI from a Fulton County, Georgia warehouse in January. U.S. District Judge J.P. Boulee, in a 68-page ruling, found that while the January seizure "was certainly not perfect," Fulton County had not established that its constitutional rights were callously disregarded or that it would suffer irreparable harm, particularly since the DOJ had provided the county with copies of the seized materials.

The Justice Department has said it is investigating "irregularities" in the 2020 election in Fulton County and cited two potential statutory violations — one requiring election records to be maintained for 22 months, another prohibiting fraudulent ballot procurement or tabulation. Georgia's 2020 presidential results were counted three times, including once by hand, with each count affirming Joe Biden's victory. Fulton County Board of Commissioners Chairman Robb Pitts said he "strongly disagrees" with the ruling and that the county intends to pursue "all available legal options."

The ruling comes alongside a separate DOJ grand jury subpoena, issued in April, seeking the names and personal contact information of all Fulton County election workers and volunteers involved in the 2020 election. The county filed a motion Monday to quash that subpoena, arguing it is overly broad and amounts to harassment of political opponents. Supporters of the investigation argue federal oversight is warranted to ensure election integrity; critics, including county officials and civil liberties advocates, contend the effort is a politically motivated attempt to intimidate election workers and relitigate a settled election.
